﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ These are two interrogative clauses, neither of which is grammatically connected to the other. Ask them first about what they have established and confirmed, an interrogative of denial; and second, an interrogative of wonder at this judgment they have passed. The meaning: what has become established for you? How do you judge for Allah the daughters, who are the category you dislike, and for yourselves the sons, who are the category you love?

﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ That is: will you not remember, with one of the two tā's deleted? The meaning: will you not take heed and reflect, so that you remember the falsehood of your statement?

﴿Or have you a manifest authority?﴾ That is: a clear, evident proof for what you say. This is a turn from one rebuke to another and a transition from one reproach to another.

﴿Then bring your Book, if you are truthful.﴾ That is: bring your clear proof for this, if you are truthful in what you say; or bring the book that speaks to you with the proof and contains it.

﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship.﴾ Most of the exegetes said: the intended meaning of "the jinn" here is the angels; it was said they are called jinn because they are not seen.

Mujahid said: they are a clan among the clans of the angels called "the jinn." Abu Malik said: they were only called "the jinn" because they are guardians of the gardens (jinan). And "kinship" (nasab) means marriage by alliance. Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: they said—may Allah curse them—"Allah has intermarried with the jinn, so the angels are their offspring." Both said: the one who makes this claim is the Jews.

Mujahid, al-Suddi and Muqatil said: the one who says this is Kinanah and Khuza'ah; they claimed that Allah proposed to the chiefs of the jinn and they married Him to the noblest of their daughters, so the angels are the daughters of Allah from the noblest of the daughters of the jinn.

Al-Hasan said: they associated Satan with the worship of Allah, and that is the kinship they assigned.

Then Allah—glorified is He—refuted them by His saying: ﴿But the jinn know that they will surely be brought forth.﴾ That is: they know that these disbelievers who made this statement will be brought forth to the Fire and punished therein.

It was also said: "the jinn knew that they themselves would be brought forth for reckoning."

The first is preferable, because when "bringing forth" (ihdar) is used without qualification, what is meant is punishment. It was also said the meaning is: "the jinn know that they will surely be brought forth to the Garden."

Then He—glorified is He—declared Himself free of what they describe, saying: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe,﴾ or it is a report of the declaring-free of the dominion of Allah—Mighty and Majestic is He—from what the polytheists have attributed to Him.

The exception in His saying: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), and the implied meaning is: "but the sincere servants of Allah are free from describing Allah with any of that." It has been read with fatha and kasra of the lam, and their meanings are as we have explained shortly. It was also said it is an exception from "those brought forth," meaning: they will be brought forth to the Fire except whoever was sincere; in that case it is connected (muttasil), not disjunctive, and on this view the sentence of glorification is parenthetical.

Then He addressed the disbelievers in general, or the disbelievers of Makkah specifically, saying: ﴿So indeed you and what you worship are not able to tempt [anyone] away.﴾ That is: indeed you and your gods whom you worship besides Allah are not able to tempt against Allah by corrupting His servants and misleading them. The word "against" ('ala) is linked to "tempting" (fatinin). The waw in "and what you worship" is either a conjunction with the subject of inna, or it means "together with" (ma'a); "what" is either a relative pronoun or a verbal noun, meaning: you and the one you worship, or your worship. The word fatinin means misleading, as one says: fatantu al-rajul and aftantuhu, and one says: fatana fulan 'ala fulan imra'atahu, meaning he corrupted her against him. So fitnah here means misleading and corrupting.

Al-Farra' said: the people of the Hijaz say "fatantuhu," and the people of Najd say "aftantuhu."

Muqatil said: he says: you do not mislead anyone with your gods except whom Allah has decreed to burn in the Blazing Fire. The "ma" in "and you are not" is negating, and "you" is addressed to them and to those they worship, by way of prevalence (taghlib).

Al-Zajjaj said: as far as I know, the exegetes are unanimous that the meaning is: you do not mislead anyone except whom Allah—Mighty and Majestic is He—has decreed that he go astray. Among this is the poet's saying:

"He turned back his scheme against him with his own temptation, and he was a misleader against us."

meaning: one who misleads.

﴿Except him who is to burn in the Blazing Fire.﴾ The majority read "ṣāl" with a kasra on the lam, because it is a defective noun in construct, the yā' being dropped due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, and it is taken according to the wording of "man," and it is singular as "huwa" is singular.

al-Hasan and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read with a damma on the lam followed by a waw, and it was reported from them that they read with a damma on the lam without a waw.

As for with the waw, it is a sound plural with waw, taken according to the meaning of "man," and the plural nun is dropped for the construct. As for without the waw, it may be a plural, and the waw was dropped in writing as it was dropped in pronunciation; and it may be singular, and by this its correct vowel would be a kasra on the lam.

al-Nahhas said: the community of exegetes say that it is a grammatical error (laḥn), because it is not permissible to say: "this is the judge of Madinah" [with a damma]. The meaning: the disbelievers and what they worship cannot mislead any of Allah's servants except him who is among the people of the Fire, namely those who persist in disbelief. Persistence in disbelief is only for one upon whom the decree of wretchedness has preceded, and he is among those who will burn in the Fire, that is, enter it.

Then the angels said, informing the Prophet—may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace—as Allah—glorified is He—related of them:

﴿There is none of us but has a known station.﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning: "there is none of us [an angel] but has a known station," or "there is none of us, an angel, except that he has a known station in the worship of Allah." It was said the implied meaning is: "there is none of us except one who has a known station." The Basrans preferred the first implied meaning, and the Kufans preferred the second.

al-Zajjaj said: this is the statement of the angels, and within it is a concealed element. The meaning: there is none of us, an angel, except that he has a known station.

Then they said: ﴿And indeed we are those who stand in ranks.﴾ That is: in positions of obedience. Qatadah said: they are the angels who arrange their feet in rows. Al-Kalbi said: the rows of the angels in the heaven are like the rows of the people of this world on earth.

﴿And indeed we are those who glorify.﴾ That is: those who declare Allah free [of imperfection] and sanctify Him from what the polytheists attribute to Him. It was also said: "those who pray." It was also said: the intended meaning of their words "those who glorify" is the totality of glorification by the tongue and by prayer. The purpose is that these attributes are the attributes of the angels, and they are not as the disbelievers described them, that they are daughters of Allah.

﴿And indeed they were saying﴾ This is a return to reporting about the polytheists, that is: before the Muhammadan mission, whenever they were overcome by ignorance they would say: ﴿If we had with us a reminder from the earlier ones,﴾ that is: a book from the books of the earlier peoples, such as the Torah and the Gospel, ﴿we would surely have been sincere servants of Allah.﴾ That is: we would have devoted worship to Him and would not have disbelieved in Him.

In His saying "and indeed they were saying," the "in" is the light (mukhaffafah) form of the heavy (thaqilah), in which there is a deleted pronoun of the matter, and the lam is the one that distinguishes it from the negating "in"; that is: indeed the matter was that the disbelievers of the Arabs would say, etc.

The fa' in His saying: ﴿But they disbelieved in it﴾ is the fa' of result (fasihah), indicating a deleted element implied in the speech.

al-Farra' said: its implied meaning is: "then Muhammad came to them with the Reminder, but they disbelieved in it," and this is in the manner of wonder at them.

﴿So they will come to know﴾ That is: the outcome of their disbelief and its end. In this is a severe threat to them.

The clause ﴿And indeed Our word had already preceded for Our servants, the messengers﴾ is a resumed sentence confirming the threat. The "word" means what Allah promised them of victory and triumph over the disbelievers.

Muqatil said: by "the word" He meant His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "Surely I shall prevail, I and My messengers."﴾ [Al-Mujadilah: 21]. al-Farra' said: "Our word preceded with happiness for them." The more preferable view is to interpret this word by what is mentioned here, for He said: ﴿Indeed they are the ones who will be helped, and indeed Our host, they are the ones who will be victorious.﴾ So this word mentioned earlier and this is its explanation. By "the host of Allah" is meant His party, namely the messengers and their followers.

al-Shaybani said: it came here in the plural form: that is, His saying ﴿they are the ones who will be victorious﴾ is because it is the end of a verse. This promise to them of victory and triumph is not contradicted by their defeat in some battles or by the triumph of the disbelievers over them, for the prevailing outcome in every encounter is their victory over the enemies and their triumph over them. So the speech came in the manner of what is usual, and the praiseworthy end is theirs in every condition and in every encounter, as He—glorified is He—said: ﴿And the good end is for the God-fearing.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 128].

Then Allah—glorified is He—commanded His Messenger to turn away from them and to overlook what proceeds from them of ignorance and misguidance, saying: ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ That is: turn away from them for a period known to Allah—glorified is He—which is the period of refraining from fighting. al-Suddi and Mujahid said: until We command you to fight. Qatadah said: until death. It was also said: until the day of Badr; it was also said: until the day of the conquest of Makkah; it was also said: this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿And see them, for they will [soon] see.﴾ That is: and watch them when punishment descends upon them through killing and capture, for they will [soon] see when seeing will not benefit them. He expressed the nearness of the matter by "seeing," that is: they will see in the near future.

It was also said: the meaning is: they will see the punishment on the Day of Resurrection.

Then He, glorified is He, threatened them with His saying: ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ They used to say, out of excessive denial, "When is this punishment?"

﴿But when it descends upon their courtyard﴾ means: when the punishment of Allah descends upon them in their open area. In the language, *al-sahah* (the courtyard) is the wide open space in front of a house. Al-Farra' said: "Nazala bi-sahatihim" and "nazala bihim" have the same meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: The punishment of these people was by killing. It was said that what is meant is the descent of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) into their courtyard on the day of the conquest of Makkah.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *nazala* in the active form. Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read it in the passive form, with the prepositional phrase acting as the subject. ﴿Evil is the morning of those who were warned﴾ means: wretched is the morning of those who were warned of the punishment. The object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: their morning.

He singled out the morning for mention because the punishment used to come upon them in it.

Then, glorified is He, repeated what had preceded, as an emphasis of the promise of punishment, and said: ﴿So turn away from them for a time, and watch, for they will [soon] see.﴾ The object of *absir* (watch) is omitted here, while it was mentioned earlier. This may be either because the earlier mention indicates it, so it is left out here for brevity, or intentionally, for generality, to signal that what they will see of the kinds of their punishment cannot be encompassed by description.

It was said: this sentence is meant to describe the conditions of the Resurrection, while the first sentence refers to their punishment in this world. On this view, it is not a case of emphasis (*ta'kid*) but of establishing a new meaning (*ta'sis*).

Then He, glorified is He, declared Himself free from the ugly things that they say, and said: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe.﴾ *Al-'izzah* means dominance and power. What is meant is His exaltation above everything they attribute to Him that is not fitting to His noble majesty. And "the Lord of Might" is an appositive (*badal*) of "your Lord."

Then He mentioned what indicates the honouring and dignifying of His messengers, and said: ﴿And peace be upon the messengers.﴾ That is, those whom He sent to His servants and who conveyed His messages. This is from *al-salam*, which is greeting. It was also said: its meaning is security for them and safety from what is disliked.

﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ This is a guidance for His servants to praise Him for sending His messengers to them as bearers of good news and warners, and a teaching to them of how to act when He bestows His favour upon them and what to say in praising Him for it. It was also said that it is praise for the destruction of the polytheists and the victory of the messengers over them. The better view is that it is praise to Allah, glorified is He, for everything He has bestowed upon all of His creation, as the omission of the object of praise indicates, since omitting it implies generality, as is established in the science of meanings (*'ilm al-ma'ani*). Praise (*al-hamd*) is good commendation with the intention of exalting.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a lineage﴾ that he said: the enemies of Allah claimed that He, blessed and exalted, and Iblis were brothers.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning His saying: ﴿So indeed you, and what you worship﴾ that he said: "So indeed you, O assembly of polytheists, and what you worship," meaning the gods. ﴿You cannot lead astray [anyone] against Him﴾ he said: "to lead astray." ﴿Except one who is to burn in Hellfire﴾ he said: it means, except one who, in My knowledge, has already been destined to burn in Hellfire.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him, concerning the verse, that he said: You will not go astray, nor will I lead astray any of you, except one for whom I have decreed that he will burn in Hellfire.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him, concerning the verse, that he said: "You will not be tempted, except one who is to burn in Hellfire."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from him, concerning His saying: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ that he said: the angels said it. ﴿And indeed we are the ones who line up﴾ the angels said it. ﴿And indeed we are the ones who glorify﴾ he said: the angels said it.

Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi in the *Kitab al-Salah*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no place in the heaven the size of a foot except that upon it is an angel prostrating or standing," and that is the saying of the angels: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station. And indeed we are the ones who line up.﴾

Muhammad ibn Nasr and Ibn 'Asakir reported from al-'Ala' ibn Sa'd that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once said to his companions: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak; there is not a place in it the size of a foot except that upon it is an angel bowing or prostrating." Then he recited: ﴿And indeed we are the ones who line up, and indeed we are the ones who glorify.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Indeed, among the heavens there is a heaven in which there is not a space the size of a handspan except that upon it is the forehead of an angel or his feet, standing or prostrating." Then he recited: ﴿And indeed we are the ones who line up, and indeed we are the ones who glorify.﴾

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as good, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I see what you do not see, and I hear what you do not hear. The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. There is not a place of four fingers' width except that an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah." It is firmly established in the *Sahih* and elsewhere that the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the Companions to form rows as the angels form their rows before their Lord. They said: "And how do the angels form their rows before their Lord?" He said: "They complete the front rows and press shoulder to shoulder in the row."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿If only we had with us a reminder from the former peoples﴾ that he said: when the polytheists of Makkah were given the reminder of the former peoples and the knowledge of the later ones, they disbelieved in the Book. ﴿But soon they will know.﴾

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) attacked Khaybar at dawn, and they had gone out with their spades. When they saw him, they said: 'Muhammad and the army!' He said: 'Allahu Akbar! Khaybar is ruined! Indeed, when we descend into the courtyard of a people, evil is the morning of those who were warned.'" This is the hadith.

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Mardawayh reported through the chain of Sa'id from Qatada from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you greet the messengers, then greet me too, for I am only a human among the messengers."

Ibn Mardawayh reported through the chain of Abu al-'Awwam from Qatada from Anas, as a raised (*marfu'*) report, something similar to it but longer than it.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whenever he wished to conclude his prayer with the greeting, would say: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

al-Tabarani reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "We used to know the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had finished the prayer by his saying: 'Glory be to your Lord' up to the end of the verse."

al-Khatib reported something similar from the hadith of Abu Sa'id.

al-Tabarani reported from Zayd ibn Arqam, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever says after every prayer: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds⁠﴾ three times, he has measured out the reward with the fullest measure."

Humayd ibn Zanjawayh in his *Targhib* reported from the chain of al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah from Ali ibn Abi Talib something similar.

Here the third part of this blessed commentary ends, by the help of Allah, accepted by the grace of Allah, written by its humble author Muhammad ibn Ali al-Shawkani, may Allah forgive both of them, on the afternoon of Thursday, the twenty-first of the sacred month of Muharram, in the year one thousand two hundred and twenty-nine of the Prophetic Hijrah, praising Allah, thanking Him, and invoking blessings and peace upon His Messenger and his family. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 37, verse 149–182 (part 1 of 2):

When Quraysh and some Arab tribes claimed that the angels are the daughters of Allah, Allah—glorified is He—commanded His Messenger—may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace—to question them in a manner of rebuke and reproach, so He said: ﴿So ask them﴾ O Muhammad, that is: inquire of them. ﴿Has your Lord then daughters while they have sons?﴾ That is: how do they assign to Allah, on the supposition of the truth of what they claim, a falsehood, the lesser of the two sexes and the lowliest of them, which is the females, while for themselves is the higher and more exalted of them, which is the males? Is this not an unjust division, due to the weakness of their minds and the badness of their understanding? A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him? That, then, is an unjust division.﴾ [An-Najm: 21–22].

Then He increased their rebuke and reproach, saying: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ Thus He turned away from the first statement to something more severe in rebuke and mockery of them. That is: how did they make them females when they were not present at their creation? This is like His saying: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 19]. So He—glorified is He—made clear that such a matter is known only through witnessing, and they did not witness it; nor is there any evidence from revelation for their claim, nor is it something perceived by reason, so that they could attribute its knowledge to their intellects.

Then Allah—glorified is He—informed about their lie, saying: ﴿Surely they say, out of their own fabrication, "Allah has begotten," and surely they are liars.﴾ So He made clear that their statement is from fabrication and invention without any evidence or even the semblance of evidence, for He neither begets nor is begotten.

The majority read ﴿walada Allahu﴾ as a verb in the past tense attributed to Allah. It was also read with walad in the genitive construction referring to Allah, as the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning: they say the angels are the child of Allah. The word walad here is in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), and it is the same for the singular, dual, plural, masculine and feminine.

Then He repeated their rebuke and reproach, saying: ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ The majority read the hamza with a fatha, as an interrogative of denunciation, and the hamza of connection (hamzat al-wasl) has been dropped with it, being dispensed with by it.

Nafi' in one narration, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, and al-A'mash read it with a hamza of connection which is pronounced at the beginning and dropped in continuous speech, and the interrogative is then implied; this was stated by al-Farra'.

Its interrogative particle is deleted because it is known from the context; or [the phrase] "chose daughters over sons" is a substitute (badal) for the clause reported by the verb "they say". And on the supposition that there is no interrogative and no substitution...

Indeed a group of the verifiers, among them al-Farra', related that rebuke may occur with an interrogative and without an interrogative, as in His saying: ﴿You used up your good things in your worldly life﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 20]. It was also said that it is by implying a verb of saying.

﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ These are two interrogative clauses, neither of which is grammatically connected to the other. Ask them first about what they have established and confirmed, an interrogative of denial; and second, an interrogative of wonder at this judgment they have passed. The meaning: what has become established for you? How do you judge for Allah the daughters, who are the category you dislike, and for yourselves the sons, who are the category you love?

﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ That is: will you not remember, with one of the two tā's deleted? The meaning: will you not take heed and reflect, so that you remember the falsehood of your statement?

﴿Or have you a manifest authority?﴾ That is: a clear, evident proof for what you say. This is a turn from one rebuke to another and a transition from one reproach to another.

﴿Then bring your Book, if you are truthful.﴾ That is: bring your clear proof for this, if you are truthful in what you say; or bring the book that speaks to you with the proof and contains it.

﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship.﴾ Most of the exegetes said: the intended meaning of "the jinn" here is the angels; it was said they are called jinn because they are not seen.

Mujahid said: they are a clan among the clans of the angels called "the jinn." Abu Malik said: they were only called "the jinn" because they are guardians of the gardens (jinan). And "kinship" (nasab) means marriage by alliance. Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: they said—may Allah curse them—"Allah has intermarried with the jinn, so the angels are their offspring." Both said: the one who makes this claim is the Jews.

Mujahid, al-Suddi and Muqatil said: the one who says this is Kinanah and Khuza'ah; they claimed that Allah proposed to the chiefs of the jinn and they married Him to the noblest of their daughters, so the angels are the daughters of Allah from the noblest of the daughters of the jinn.

Al-Hasan said: they associated Satan with the worship of Allah, and that is the kinship they assigned.

Then Allah—glorified is He—refuted them by His saying: ﴿But the jinn know that they will surely be brought forth.﴾ That is: they know that these disbelievers who made this statement will be brought forth to the Fire and punished therein.

It was also said: "the jinn knew that they themselves would be brought forth for reckoning."

The first is preferable, because when "bringing forth" (ihdar) is used without qualification, what is meant is punishment. It was also said the meaning is: "the jinn know that they will surely be brought forth to the Garden."

Then He—glorified is He—declared Himself free of what they describe, saying: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe,﴾ or it is a report of the declaring-free of the dominion of Allah—Mighty and Majestic is He—from what the polytheists have attributed to Him.

The exception in His saying: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), and the implied meaning is: "but the sincere servants of Allah are free from describing Allah with any of that." It has been read with fatha and kasra of the lam, and their meanings are as we have explained shortly. It was also said it is an exception from "those brought forth," meaning: they will be brought forth to the Fire except whoever was sincere; in that case it is connected (muttasil), not disjunctive, and on this view the sentence of glorification is parenthetical.

Then He addressed the disbelievers in general, or the disbelievers of Makkah specifically, saying: ﴿So indeed you and what you worship are not able to tempt [anyone] away.﴾ That is: indeed you and your gods whom you worship besides Allah are not able to tempt against Allah by corrupting His servants and misleading them. The word "against" ('ala) is linked to "tempting" (fatinin). The waw in "and what you worship" is either a conjunction with the subject of inna, or it means "together with" (ma'a); "what" is either a relative pronoun or a verbal noun, meaning: you and the one you worship, or your worship. The word fatinin means misleading, as one says: fatantu al-rajul and aftantuhu, and one says: fatana fulan 'ala fulan imra'atahu, meaning he corrupted her against him. So fitnah here means misleading and corrupting.

Al-Farra' said: the people of the Hijaz say "fatantuhu," and the people of Najd say "aftantuhu."

Muqatil said: he says: you do not mislead anyone with your gods except whom Allah has decreed to burn in the Blazing Fire. The "ma" in "and you are not" is negating, and "you" is addressed to them and to those they worship, by way of prevalence (taghlib).

Al-Zajjaj said: as far as I know, the exegetes are unanimous that the meaning is: you do not mislead anyone except whom Allah—Mighty and Majestic is He—has decreed that he go astray. Among this is the poet's saying:

"He turned back his scheme against him with his own temptation, and he was a misleader against us."

meaning: one who misleads.

﴿Except him who is to burn in the Blazing Fire.﴾ The majority read "ṣāl" with a kasra on the lam, because it is a defective noun in construct, the yā' being dropped due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, and it is taken according to the wording of "man," and it is singular as "huwa" is singular.

al-Hasan and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read with a damma on the lam followed by a waw, and it was reported from them that they read with a damma on the lam without a waw.

As for with the waw, it is a sound plural with waw, taken according to the meaning of "man," and the plural nun is dropped for the construct. As for without the waw, it may be a plural, and the waw was dropped in writing as it was dropped in pronunciation; and it may be singular, and by this its correct vowel would be a kasra on the lam.

al-Nahhas said: the community of exegetes say that it is a grammatical error (laḥn), because it is not permissible to say: "this is the judge of Madinah" [with a damma]. The meaning: the disbelievers and what they worship cannot mislead any of Allah's servants except him who is among the people of the Fire, namely those who persist in disbelief. Persistence in disbelief is only for one upon whom the decree of wretchedness has preceded, and he is among those who will burn in the Fire, that is, enter it.

Then the angels said, informing the Prophet—may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace—as Allah—glorified is He—related of them:

﴿There is none of us but has a known station.﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning: "there is none of us [an angel] but has a known station," or "there is none of us, an angel, except that he has a known station in the worship of Allah." It was said the implied meaning is: "there is none of us except one who has a known station." The Basrans preferred the first implied meaning, and the Kufans preferred the second.

al-Zajjaj said: this is the statement of the angels, and within it is a concealed element. The meaning: there is none of us, an angel, except that he has a known station.

Then they said: ﴿And indeed we are those who stand in ranks.﴾ That is: in positions of obedience. Qatadah said: they are the angels who arrange their feet in rows. Al-Kalbi said: the rows of the angels in the heaven are like the rows of the people of this world on earth.

﴿And indeed we are those who glorify.﴾ That is: those who declare Allah free [of imperfection] and sanctify Him from what the polytheists attribute to Him. It was also said: "those who pray." It was also said: the intended meaning of their words "those who glorify" is the totality of glorification by the tongue and by prayer. The purpose is that these attributes are the attributes of the angels, and they are not as the disbelievers described them, that they are daughters of Allah.

﴿And indeed they were saying﴾ This is a return to reporting about the polytheists, that is: before the Muhammadan mission, whenever they were overcome by ignorance they would say: ﴿If we had with us a reminder from the earlier ones,﴾ that is: a book from the books of the earlier peoples, such as the Torah and the Gospel, ﴿we would surely have been sincere servants of Allah.﴾ That is: we would have devoted worship to Him and would not have disbelieved in Him.

In His saying "and indeed they were saying," the "in" is the light (mukhaffafah) form of the heavy (thaqilah), in which there is a deleted pronoun of the matter, and the lam is the one that distinguishes it from the negating "in"; that is: indeed the matter was that the disbelievers of the Arabs would say, etc.

The fa' in His saying: ﴿But they disbelieved in it﴾ is the fa' of result (fasihah), indicating a deleted element implied in the speech.

al-Farra' said: its implied meaning is: "then Muhammad came to them with the Reminder, but they disbelieved in it," and this is in the manner of wonder at them.

﴿So they will come to know﴾ That is: the outcome of their disbelief and its end. In this is a severe threat to them.

The clause ﴿And indeed Our word had already preceded for Our servants, the messengers﴾ is a resumed sentence confirming the threat. The "word" means what Allah promised them of victory and triumph over the disbelievers.

Muqatil said: by "the word" He meant His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "Surely I shall prevail, I and My messengers."﴾ [Al-Mujadilah: 21]. al-Farra' said: "Our word preceded with happiness for them." The more preferable view is to interpret this word by what is mentioned here, for He said: ﴿Indeed they are the ones who will be helped, and indeed Our host, they are the ones who will be victorious.﴾ So this word mentioned earlier and this is its explanation. By "the host of Allah" is meant His party, namely the messengers and their followers.

al-Shaybani said: it came here in the plural form: that is, His saying ﴿they are the ones who will be victorious﴾ is because it is the end of a verse. This promise to them of victory and triumph is not contradicted by their defeat in some battles or by the triumph of the disbelievers over them, for the prevailing outcome in every encounter is their victory over the enemies and their triumph over them. So the speech came in the manner of what is usual, and the praiseworthy end is theirs in every condition and in every encounter, as He—glorified is He—said: ﴿And the good end is for the God-fearing.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 128].

Then Allah—glorified is He—commanded His Messenger to turn away from them and to overlook what proceeds from them of ignorance and misguidance, saying: ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ That is: turn away from them for a period known to Allah—glorified is He—which is the period of refraining from fighting. al-Suddi and Mujahid said: until We command you to fight. Qatadah said: until death. It was also said: until the day of Badr; it was also said: until the day of the conquest of Makkah; it was also said: this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿And see them, for they will [soon] see.﴾ That is: and watch them when punishment descends upon them through killing and capture, for they will [soon] see when seeing will not benefit them. He expressed the nearness of the matter by "seeing," that is: they will see in the near future.

It was also said: the meaning is: they will see the punishment on the Day of Resurrection.

Then He, glorified is He, threatened them with His saying: ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ They used to say, out of excessive denial, "When is this punishment?"

﴿But when it descends upon their courtyard﴾ means: when the punishment of Allah descends upon them in their open area. In the language, *al-sahah* (the courtyard) is the wide open space in front of a house. Al-Farra' said: "Nazala bi-sahatihim" and "nazala bihim" have the same meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: The punishment of these people was by killing. It was said that what is meant is the descent of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) into their courtyard on the day of the conquest of Makkah.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *nazala* in the active form. Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read it in the passive form, with the prepositional phrase acting as the subject. ﴿Evil is the morning of those who were warned﴾ means: wretched is the morning of those who were warned of the punishment. The object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: their morning.

He singled out the morning for mention because the punishment used to come upon them in it.

Then, glorified is He, repeated what had preceded, as an emphasis of the promise of punishment, and said: ﴿So turn away from them for a time, and watch, for they will [soon] see.﴾ The object of *absir* (watch) is omitted here, while it was mentioned earlier. This may be either because the earlier mention indicates it, so it is left out here for brevity, or intentionally, for generality, to signal that what they will see of the kinds of their punishment cannot be encompassed by description.

It was said: this sentence is meant to describe the conditions of the Resurrection, while the first sentence refers to their punishment in this world. On this view, it is not a case of emphasis (*ta'kid*) but of establishing a new meaning (*ta'sis*).

Then He, glorified is He, declared Himself free from the ugly things that they say, and said: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe.﴾ *Al-'izzah* means dominance and power. What is meant is His exaltation above everything they attribute to Him that is not fitting to His noble majesty. And "the Lord of Might" is an appositive (*badal*) of "your Lord."

Then He mentioned what indicates the honouring and dignifying of His messengers, and said: ﴿And peace be upon the messengers.﴾ That is, those whom He sent to His servants and who conveyed His messages. This is from *al-salam*, which is greeting. It was also said: its meaning is security for them and safety from what is disliked.

﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ This is a guidance for His servants to praise Him for sending His messengers to them as bearers of good news and warners, and a teaching to them of how to act when He bestows His favour upon them and what to say in praising Him for it. It was also said that it is praise for the destruction of the polytheists and the victory of the messengers over them. The better view is that it is praise to Allah, glorified is He, for everything He has bestowed upon all of His creation, as the omission of the object of praise indicates, since omitting it implies generality, as is established in the science of meanings (*'ilm al-ma'ani*). Praise (*al-hamd*) is good commendation with the intention of exalting.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a lineage﴾ that he said: the enemies of Allah claimed that He, blessed and exalted, and Iblis were brothers.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning His saying: ﴿So indeed you, and what you worship﴾ that he said: "So indeed you, O assembly of polytheists, and what you worship," meaning the gods. ﴿You cannot lead astray [anyone] against Him﴾ he said: "to lead astray." ﴿Except one who is to burn in Hellfire﴾ he said: it means, except one who, in My knowledge, has already been destined to burn in Hellfire.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him, concerning the verse, that he said: You will not go astray, nor will I lead astray any of you, except one for whom I have decreed that he will burn in Hellfire.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him, concerning the verse, that he said: "You will not be tempted, except one who is to burn in Hellfire."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from him, concerning His saying: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ that he said: the angels said it. ﴿And indeed we are the ones who line up﴾ the angels said it. ﴿And indeed we are the ones who glorify﴾ he said: the angels said it.

Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi in the *Kitab al-Salah*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no place in the heaven the size of a foot except that upon it is an angel prostrating or standing," and that is the saying of the angels: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station. And indeed we are the ones who line up.﴾

Muhammad ibn Nasr and Ibn 'Asakir reported from al-'Ala' ibn Sa'd that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once said to his companions: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak; there is not a place in it the size of a foot except that upon it is an angel bowing or prostrating." Then he recited: ﴿And indeed we are the ones who line up, and indeed we are the ones who glorify.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Indeed, among the heavens there is a heaven in which there is not a space the size of a handspan except that upon it is the forehead of an angel or his feet, standing or prostrating." Then he recited: ﴿And indeed we are the ones who line up, and indeed we are the ones who glorify.﴾

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as good, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I see what you do not see, and I hear what you do not hear. The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. There is not a place of four fingers' width except that an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah." It is firmly established in the *Sahih* and elsewhere that the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the Companions to form rows as the angels form their rows before their Lord. They said: "And how do the angels form their rows before their Lord?" He said: "They complete the front rows and press shoulder to shoulder in the row."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿If only we had with us a reminder from the former peoples﴾ that he said: when the polytheists of Makkah were given the reminder of the former peoples and the knowledge of the later ones, they disbelieved in the Book. ﴿But soon they will know.﴾

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) attacked Khaybar at dawn, and they had gone out with their spades. When they saw him, they said: 'Muhammad and the army!' He said: 'Allahu Akbar! Khaybar is ruined! Indeed, when we descend into the courtyard of a people, evil is the morning of those who were warned.'" This is the hadith.

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Mardawayh reported through the chain of Sa'id from Qatada from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you greet the messengers, then greet me too, for I am only a human among the messengers."

Ibn Mardawayh reported through the chain of Abu al-'Awwam from Qatada from Anas, as a raised (*marfu'*) report, something similar to it but longer than it.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whenever he wished to conclude his prayer with the greeting, would say: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

al-Tabarani reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "We used to know the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had finished the prayer by his saying: 'Glory be to your Lord' up to the end of the verse."

al-Khatib reported something similar from the hadith of Abu Sa'id.

al-Tabarani reported from Zayd ibn Arqam, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever says after every prayer: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds⁠﴾ three times, he has measured out the reward with the fullest measure."

Humayd ibn Zanjawayh in his *Targhib* reported from the chain of al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah from Ali ibn Abi Talib something similar.

Here the third part of this blessed commentary ends, by the help of Allah, accepted by the grace of Allah, written by its humble author Muhammad ibn Ali al-Shawkani, may Allah forgive both of them, on the afternoon of Thursday, the twenty-first of the sacred month of Muharram, in the year one thousand two hundred and twenty-nine of the Prophetic Hijrah, praising Allah, thanking Him, and invoking blessings and peace upon His Messenger and his family. After it, if Allah wills, comes the tafsir of Surah Sad.

The reading of this part was completed under its author, may Allah preserve him, on Monday, the first of Jumada al-Akhirah, in the year 1239 AH.

﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ That is: will you not remember, with one of the two tā's deleted? The meaning: will you not take heed and reflect, so that you remember the falsehood of your statement?

﴿Or have you a manifest authority?﴾ That is: a clear, evident proof for what you say. This is a turn from one rebuke to another and a transition from one reproach to another.

﴿Then bring your Book, if you are truthful.﴾ That is: bring your clear proof for this, if you are truthful in what you say; or bring the book that speaks to you with the proof and contains it.

﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship.﴾ Most of the exegetes said: the intended meaning of "the jinn" here is the angels; it was said they are called jinn because they are not seen.

Mujahid said: they are a clan among the clans of the angels called "the jinn." Abu Malik said: they were only called "the jinn" because they are guardians of the gardens (jinan). And "kinship" (nasab) means marriage by alliance. Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: they said—may Allah curse them—"Allah has intermarried with the jinn, so the angels are their offspring." Both said: the one who makes this claim is the Jews.

Mujahid, al-Suddi and Muqatil said: the one who says this is Kinanah and Khuza'ah; they claimed that Allah proposed to the chiefs of the jinn and they married Him to the noblest of their daughters, so the angels are the daughters of Allah from the noblest of the daughters of the jinn.

Al-Hasan said: they associated Satan with the worship of Allah, and that is the kinship they assigned.

Then Allah—glorified is He—refuted them by His saying: ﴿But the jinn know that they will surely be brought forth.﴾ That is: they know that these disbelievers who made this statement will be brought forth to the Fire and punished therein.

It was also said: "the jinn knew that they themselves would be brought forth for reckoning."

The first is preferable, because when "bringing forth" (ihdar) is used without qualification, what is meant is punishment. It was also said the meaning is: "the jinn know that they will surely be brought forth to the Garden."

Then He—glorified is He—declared Himself free of what they describe, saying: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe,﴾ or it is a report of the declaring-free of the dominion of Allah—Mighty and Majestic is He—from what the polytheists have attributed to Him.

The exception in His saying: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), and the implied meaning is: "but the sincere servants of Allah are free from describing Allah with any of that." It has been read with fatha and kasra of the lam, and their meanings are as we have explained shortly. It was also said it is an exception from "those brought forth," meaning: they will be brought forth to the Fire except whoever was sincere; in that case it is connected (muttasil), not disjunctive, and on this view the sentence of glorification is parenthetical.

Then He addressed the disbelievers in general, or the disbelievers of Makkah specifically, saying: ﴿So indeed you and what you worship are not able to tempt [anyone] away.﴾ That is: indeed you and your gods whom you worship besides Allah are not able to tempt against Allah by corrupting His servants and misleading them. The word "against" ('ala) is linked to "tempting" (fatinin). The waw in "and what you worship" is either a conjunction with the subject of inna, or it means "together with" (ma'a); "what" is either a relative pronoun or a verbal noun, meaning: you and the one you worship, or your worship. The word fatinin means misleading, as one says: fatantu al-rajul and aftantuhu, and one says: fatana fulan 'ala fulan imra'atahu, meaning he corrupted her against him. So fitnah here means misleading and corrupting.

Al-Farra' said: the people of the Hijaz say "fatantuhu," and the people of Najd say "aftantuhu."

Muqatil said: he says: you do not mislead anyone with your gods except whom Allah has decreed to burn in the Blazing Fire. The "ma" in "and you are not" is negating, and "you" is addressed to them and to those they worship, by way of prevalence (taghlib).

Al-Zajjaj said: as far as I know, the exegetes are unanimous that the meaning is: you do not mislead anyone except whom Allah—Mighty and Majestic is He—has decreed that he go astray. Among this is the poet's saying:

"He turned back his scheme against him with his own temptation, and he was a misleader against us."

meaning: one who misleads.

﴿Except him who is to burn in the Blazing Fire.﴾ The majority read "ṣāl" with a kasra on the lam, because it is a defective noun in construct, the yā' being dropped due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, and it is taken according to the wording of "man," and it is singular as "huwa" is singular.

al-Hasan and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read with a damma on the lam followed by a waw, and it was reported from them that they read with a damma on the lam without a waw.

As for with the waw, it is a sound plural with waw, taken according to the meaning of "man," and the plural nun is dropped for the construct. As for without the waw, it may be a plural, and the waw was dropped in writing as it was dropped in pronunciation; and it may be singular, and by this its correct vowel would be a kasra on the lam.

al-Nahhas said: the community of exegetes say that it is a grammatical error (laḥn), because it is not permissible to say: "this is the judge of Madinah" [with a damma]. The meaning: the disbelievers and what they worship cannot mislead any of Allah's servants except him who is among the people of the Fire, namely those who persist in disbelief. Persistence in disbelief is only for one upon whom the decree of wretchedness has preceded, and he is among those who will burn in the Fire, that is, enter it.

Then the angels said, informing the Prophet—may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace—as Allah—glorified is He—related of them:

﴿There is none of us but has a known station.﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning: "there is none of us [an angel] but has a known station," or "there is none of us, an angel, except that he has a known station in the worship of Allah." It was said the implied meaning is: "there is none of us except one who has a known station." The Basrans preferred the first implied meaning, and the Kufans preferred the second.

al-Zajjaj said: this is the statement of the angels, and within it is a concealed element. The meaning: there is none of us, an angel, except that he has a known station.

Then they said: ﴿And indeed we are those who stand in ranks.﴾ That is: in positions of obedience. Qatadah said: they are the angels who arrange their feet in rows. Al-Kalbi said: the rows of the angels in the heaven are like the rows of the people of this world on earth.

﴿And indeed we are those who glorify.﴾ That is: those who declare Allah free [of imperfection] and sanctify Him from what the polytheists attribute to Him. It was also said: "those who pray." It was also said: the intended meaning of their words "those who glorify" is the totality of glorification by the tongue and by prayer. The purpose is that these attributes are the attributes of the angels, and they are not as the disbelievers described them, that they are daughters of Allah.

﴿And indeed they were saying﴾ This is a return to reporting about the polytheists, that is: before the Muhammadan mission, whenever they were overcome by ignorance they would say: ﴿If we had with us a reminder from the earlier ones,﴾ that is: a book from the books of the earlier peoples, such as the Torah and the Gospel, ﴿we would surely have been sincere servants of Allah.﴾ That is: we would have devoted worship to Him and would not have disbelieved in Him.

In His saying "and indeed they were saying," the "in" is the light (mukhaffafah) form of the heavy (thaqilah), in which there is a deleted pronoun of the matter, and the lam is the one that distinguishes it from the negating "in"; that is: indeed the matter was that the disbelievers of the Arabs would say, etc.

The fa' in His saying: ﴿But they disbelieved in it﴾ is the fa' of result (fasihah), indicating a deleted element implied in the speech.

al-Farra' said: its implied meaning is: "then Muhammad came to them with the Reminder, but they disbelieved in it," and this is in the manner of wonder at them.

﴿So they will come to know﴾ That is: the outcome of their disbelief and its end. In this is a severe threat to them.

The clause ﴿And indeed Our word had already preceded for Our servants, the messengers﴾ is a resumed sentence confirming the threat. The "word" means what Allah promised them of victory and triumph over the disbelievers.

Muqatil said: by "the word" He meant His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "Surely I shall prevail, I and My messengers."﴾ [Al-Mujadilah: 21]. al-Farra' said: "Our word preceded with happiness for them." The more preferable view is to interpret this word by what is mentioned here, for He said: ﴿Indeed they are the ones who will be helped, and indeed Our host, they are the ones who will be victorious.﴾ So this word mentioned earlier and this is its explanation. By "the host of Allah" is meant His party, namely the messengers and their followers.

al-Shaybani said: it came here in the plural form: that is, His saying ﴿they are the ones who will be victorious﴾ is because it is the end of a verse. This promise to them of victory and triumph is not contradicted by their defeat in some battles or by the triumph of the disbelievers over them, for the prevailing outcome in every encounter is their victory over the enemies and their triumph over them. So the speech came in the manner of what is usual, and the praiseworthy end is theirs in every condition and in every encounter, as He—glorified is He—said: ﴿And the good end is for the God-fearing.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 128].

Then Allah—glorified is He—commanded His Messenger to turn away from them and to overlook what proceeds from them of ignorance and misguidance, saying: ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ That is: turn away from them for a period known to Allah—glorified is He—which is the period of refraining from fighting. al-Suddi and Mujahid said: until We command you to fight. Qatadah said: until death. It was also said: until the day of Badr; it was also said: until the day of the conquest of Makkah; it was also said: this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿And see them, for they will [soon] see.﴾ That is: and watch them when punishment descends upon them through killing and capture, for they will [soon] see when seeing will not benefit them. He expressed the nearness of the matter by "seeing," that is: they will see in the near future.

It was also said: the meaning is: they will see the punishment on the Day of Resurrection.

Then He, glorified is He, threatened them with His saying: ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ They used to say, out of excessive denial, "When is this punishment?"

﴿But when it descends upon their courtyard﴾ means: when the punishment of Allah descends upon them in their open area. In the language, *al-sahah* (the courtyard) is the wide open space in front of a house. Al-Farra' said: "Nazala bi-sahatihim" and "nazala bihim" have the same meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: The punishment of these people was by killing. It was said that what is meant is the descent of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) into their courtyard on the day of the conquest of Makkah.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *nazala* in the active form. Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read it in the passive form, with the prepositional phrase acting as the subject. ﴿Evil is the morning of those who were warned﴾ means: wretched is the morning of those who were warned of the punishment. The object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: their morning.

He singled out the morning for mention because the punishment used to come upon them in it.

Then, glorified is He, repeated what had preceded, as an emphasis of the promise of punishment, and said: ﴿So turn away from them for a time, and watch, for they will [soon] see.﴾ The object of *absir* (watch) is omitted here, while it was mentioned earlier. This may be either because the earlier mention indicates it, so it is left out here for brevity, or intentionally, for generality, to signal that what they will see of the kinds of their punishment cannot be encompassed by description.

It was said: this sentence is meant to describe the conditions of the Resurrection, while the first sentence refers to their punishment in this world. On this view, it is not a case of emphasis (*ta'kid*) but of establishing a new meaning (*ta'sis*).

Then He, glorified is He, declared Himself free from the ugly things that they say, and said: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe.﴾ *Al-'izzah* means dominance and power. What is meant is His exaltation above everything they attribute to Him that is not fitting to His noble majesty. And "the Lord of Might" is an appositive (*badal*) of "your Lord."

Then He mentioned what indicates the honouring and dignifying of His messengers, and said: ﴿And peace be upon the messengers.﴾ That is, those whom He sent to His servants and who conveyed His messages. This is from *al-salam*, which is greeting. It was also said: its meaning is security for them and safety from what is disliked.

﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ This is a guidance for His servants to praise Him for sending His messengers to them as bearers of good news and warners, and a teaching to them of how to act when He bestows His favour upon them and what to say in praising Him for it. It was also said that it is praise for the destruction of the polytheists and the victory of the messengers over them. The better view is that it is praise to Allah, glorified is He, for everything He has bestowed upon all of His creation, as the omission of the object of praise indicates, since omitting it implies generality, as is established in the science of meanings (*'ilm al-ma'ani*). Praise (*al-hamd*) is good commendation with the intention of exalting.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a lineage﴾ that he said: the enemies of Allah claimed that He, blessed and exalted, and Iblis were brothers.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning His saying: ﴿So indeed you, and what you worship﴾ that he said: "So indeed you, O assembly of polytheists, and what you worship," meaning the gods. ﴿You cannot lead astray [anyone] against Him﴾ he said: "to lead astray." ﴿Except one who is to burn in Hellfire﴾ he said: it means, except one who, in My knowledge, has already been destined to burn in Hellfire.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him, concerning the verse, that he said: You will not go astray, nor will I lead astray any of you, except one for whom I have decreed that he will burn in Hellfire.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him, concerning the verse, that he said: "You will not be tempted, except one who is to burn in Hellfire."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from him, concerning His saying: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ that he said: the angels said it. ﴿And indeed we are the ones who line up﴾ the angels said it. ﴿And indeed we are the ones who glorify﴾ he said: the angels said it.

Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi in the *Kitab al-Salah*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no place in the heaven the size of a foot except that upon it is an angel prostrating or standing," and that is the saying of the angels: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station. And indeed we are the ones who line up.﴾

Muhammad ibn Nasr and Ibn 'Asakir reported from al-'Ala' ibn Sa'd that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once said to his companions: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak; there is not a place in it the size of a foot except that upon it is an angel bowing or prostrating." Then he recited: ﴿And indeed we are the ones who line up, and indeed we are the ones who glorify.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Indeed, among the heavens there is a heaven in which there is not a space the size of a handspan except that upon it is the forehead of an angel or his feet, standing or prostrating." Then he recited: ﴿And indeed we are the ones who line up, and indeed we are the ones who glorify.﴾

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as good, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I see what you do not see, and I hear what you do not hear. The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. There is not a place of four fingers' width except that an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah." It is firmly established in the *Sahih* and elsewhere that the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the Companions to form rows as the angels form their rows before their Lord. They said: "And how do the angels form their rows before their Lord?" He said: "They complete the front rows and press shoulder to shoulder in the row."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿If only we had with us a reminder from the former peoples﴾ that he said: when the polytheists of Makkah were given the reminder of the former peoples and the knowledge of the later ones, they disbelieved in the Book. ﴿But soon they will know.﴾

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) attacked Khaybar at dawn, and they had gone out with their spades. When they saw him, they said: 'Muhammad and the army!' He said: 'Allahu Akbar! Khaybar is ruined! Indeed, when we descend into the courtyard of a people, evil is the morning of those who were warned.'" This is the hadith.

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Mardawayh reported through the chain of Sa'id from Qatada from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you greet the messengers, then greet me too, for I am only a human among the messengers."

Ibn Mardawayh reported through the chain of Abu al-'Awwam from Qatada from Anas, as a raised (*marfu'*) report, something similar to it but longer than it.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whenever he wished to conclude his prayer with the greeting, would say: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

al-Tabarani reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "We used to know the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had finished the prayer by his saying: 'Glory be to your Lord' up to the end of the verse."

al-Khatib reported something similar from the hadith of Abu Sa'id.

al-Tabarani reported from Zayd ibn Arqam, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever says after every prayer: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds⁠﴾ three times, he has measured out the reward with the fullest measure."

Humayd ibn Zanjawayh in his *Targhib* reported from the chain of al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah from Ali ibn Abi Talib something similar.

Here the third part of this blessed commentary ends, by the help of Allah, accepted by the grace of Allah, written by its humble author Muhammad ibn Ali al-Shawkani, may Allah forgive both of them, on the afternoon of Thursday, the twenty-first of the sacred month of Muharram, in the year one thousand two hundred and twenty-nine of the Prophetic Hijrah, praising Allah, thanking Him, and invoking blessings and peace upon His Messenger and his family. After it, if Allah wills, comes the tafsir of Surah Sad.

The reading of this part was completed under its author, may Allah preserve him, on Monday, the first of Jumada al-Akhirah, in the year 1239 AH.

Written by Yahya ibn Ali al-Shawkani, may Allah forgive both of them.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 37, verse 149–182 (part 1 of 2):

When Quraysh and some Arab tribes claimed that the angels are the daughters of Allah, Allah—glorified is He—commanded His Messenger—may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace—to question them in a manner of rebuke and reproach, so He said: ﴿So ask them﴾ O Muhammad, that is: inquire of them. ﴿Has your Lord then daughters while they have sons?﴾ That is: how do they assign to Allah, on the supposition of the truth of what they claim, a falsehood, the lesser of the two sexes and the lowliest of them, which is the females, while for themselves is the higher and more exalted of them, which is the males? Is this not an unjust division, due to the weakness of their minds and the badness of their understanding? A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him? That, then, is an unjust division.﴾ [An-Najm: 21–22].

Then He increased their rebuke and reproach, saying: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ Thus He turned away from the first statement to something more severe in rebuke and mockery of them. That is: how did they make them females when they were not present at their creation? This is like His saying: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 19]. So He—glorified is He—made clear that such a matter is known only through witnessing, and they did not witness it; nor is there any evidence from revelation for their claim, nor is it something perceived by reason, so that they could attribute its knowledge to their intellects.

Then Allah—glorified is He—informed about their lie, saying: ﴿Surely they say, out of their own fabrication, "Allah has begotten," and surely they are liars.﴾ So He made clear that their statement is from fabrication and invention without any evidence or even the semblance of evidence, for He neither begets nor is begotten.

The majority read ﴿walada Allahu﴾ as a verb in the past tense attributed to Allah. It was also read with walad in the genitive construction referring to Allah, as the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning: they say the angels are the child of Allah. The word walad here is in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), and it is the same for the singular, dual, plural, masculine and feminine.

Then He repeated their rebuke and reproach, saying: ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ The majority read the hamza with a fatha, as an interrogative of denunciation, and the hamza of connection (hamzat al-wasl) has been dropped with it, being dispensed with by it.

Nafi' in one narration, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, and al-A'mash read it with a hamza of connection which is pronounced at the beginning and dropped in continuous speech, and the interrogative is then implied; this was stated by al-Farra'.

Its interrogative particle is deleted because it is known from the context; or [the phrase] "chose daughters over sons" is a substitute (badal) for the clause reported by the verb "they say". And on the supposition that there is no interrogative and no substitution...

Indeed a group of the verifiers, among them al-Farra', related that rebuke may occur with an interrogative and without an interrogative, as in His saying: ﴿You used up your good things in your worldly life﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 20]. It was also said that it is by implying a verb of saying.

﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ These are two interrogative clauses, neither of which is grammatically connected to the other. Ask them first about what they have established and confirmed, an interrogative of denial; and second, an interrogative of wonder at this judgment they have passed. The meaning: what has become established for you? How do you judge for Allah the daughters, who are the category you dislike, and for yourselves the sons, who are the category you love?

﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ That is: will you not remember, with one of the two tā's deleted? The meaning: will you not take heed and reflect, so that you remember the falsehood of your statement?

﴿Or have you a manifest authority?﴾ That is: a clear, evident proof for what you say. This is a turn from one rebuke to another and a transition from one reproach to another.

﴿Then bring your Book, if you are truthful.﴾ That is: bring your clear proof for this, if you are truthful in what you say; or bring the book that speaks to you with the proof and contains it.

﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship.﴾ Most of the exegetes said: the intended meaning of "the jinn" here is the angels; it was said they are called jinn because they are not seen.

Mujahid said: they are a clan among the clans of the angels called "the jinn." Abu Malik said: they were only called "the jinn" because they are guardians of the gardens (jinan). And "kinship" (nasab) means marriage by alliance. Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: they said—may Allah curse them—"Allah has intermarried with the jinn, so the angels are their offspring." Both said: the one who makes this claim is the Jews.

Mujahid, al-Suddi and Muqatil said: the one who says this is Kinanah and Khuza'ah; they claimed that Allah proposed to the chiefs of the jinn and they married Him to the noblest of their daughters, so the angels are the daughters of Allah from the noblest of the daughters of the jinn.

Al-Hasan said: they associated Satan with the worship of Allah, and that is the kinship they assigned.

Then Allah—glorified is He—refuted them by His saying: ﴿But the jinn know that they will surely be brought forth.﴾ That is: they know that these disbelievers who made this statement will be brought forth to the Fire and punished therein.

It was also said: "the jinn knew that they themselves would be brought forth for reckoning."

The first is preferable, because when "bringing forth" (ihdar) is used without qualification, what is meant is punishment. It was also said the meaning is: "the jinn know that they will surely be brought forth to the Garden."

Then He—glorified is He—declared Himself free of what they describe, saying: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe,﴾ or it is a report of the declaring-free of the dominion of Allah—Mighty and Majestic is He—from what the polytheists have attributed to Him.

The exception in His saying: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), and the implied meaning is: "but the sincere servants of Allah are free from describing Allah with any of that." It has been read with fatha and kasra of the lam, and their meanings are as we have explained shortly. It was also said it is an exception from "those brought forth," meaning: they will be brought forth to the Fire except whoever was sincere; in that case it is connected (muttasil), not disjunctive, and on this view the sentence of glorification is parenthetical.

Then He addressed the disbelievers in general, or the disbelievers of Makkah specifically, saying: ﴿So indeed you and what you worship are not able to tempt [anyone] away.﴾ That is: indeed you and your gods whom you worship besides Allah are not able to tempt against Allah by corrupting His servants and misleading them. The word "against" ('ala) is linked to "tempting" (fatinin). The waw in "and what you worship" is either a conjunction with the subject of inna, or it means "together with" (ma'a); "what" is either a relative pronoun or a verbal noun, meaning: you and the one you worship, or your worship. The word fatinin means misleading, as one says: fatantu al-rajul and aftantuhu, and one says: fatana fulan 'ala fulan imra'atahu, meaning he corrupted her against him. So fitnah here means misleading and corrupting.

Al-Farra' said: the people of the Hijaz say "fatantuhu," and the people of Najd say "aftantuhu."

Muqatil said: he says: you do not mislead anyone with your gods except whom Allah has decreed to burn in the Blazing Fire. The "ma" in "and you are not" is negating, and "you" is addressed to them and to those they worship, by way of prevalence (taghlib).

Al-Zajjaj said: as far as I know, the exegetes are unanimous that the meaning is: you do not mislead anyone except whom Allah—Mighty and Majestic is He—has decreed that he go astray. Among this is the poet's saying:

"He turned back his scheme against him with his own temptation, and he was a misleader against us."

meaning: one who misleads.

﴿Except him who is to burn in the Blazing Fire.﴾ The majority read "ṣāl" with a kasra on the lam, because it is a defective noun in construct, the yā' being dropped due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, and it is taken according to the wording of "man," and it is singular as "huwa" is singular.

al-Hasan and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read with a damma on the lam followed by a waw, and it was reported from them that they read with a damma on the lam without a waw.

As for with the waw, it is a sound plural with waw, taken according to the meaning of "man," and the plural nun is dropped for the construct. As for without the waw, it may be a plural, and the waw was dropped in writing as it was dropped in pronunciation; and it may be singular, and by this its correct vowel would be a kasra on the lam.

al-Nahhas said: the community of exegetes say that it is a grammatical error (laḥn), because it is not permissible to say: "this is the judge of Madinah" [with a damma]. The meaning: the disbelievers and what they worship cannot mislead any of Allah's servants except him who is among the people of the Fire, namely those who persist in disbelief. Persistence in disbelief is only for one upon whom the decree of wretchedness has preceded, and he is among those who will burn in the Fire, that is, enter it.

Then the angels said, informing the Prophet—may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace—as Allah—glorified is He—related of them:

﴿There is none of us but has a known station.﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning: "there is none of us [an angel] but has a known station," or "there is none of us, an angel, except that he has a known station in the worship of Allah." It was said the implied meaning is: "there is none of us except one who has a known station." The Basrans preferred the first implied meaning, and the Kufans preferred the second.

al-Zajjaj said: this is the statement of the angels, and within it is a concealed element. The meaning: there is none of us, an angel, except that he has a known station.

Then they said: ﴿And indeed we are those who stand in ranks.﴾ That is: in positions of obedience. Qatadah said: they are the angels who arrange their feet in rows. Al-Kalbi said: the rows of the angels in the heaven are like the rows of the people of this world on earth.

﴿And indeed we are those who glorify.﴾ That is: those who declare Allah free [of imperfection] and sanctify Him from what the polytheists attribute to Him. It was also said: "those who pray." It was also said: the intended meaning of their words "those who glorify" is the totality of glorification by the tongue and by prayer. The purpose is that these attributes are the attributes of the angels, and they are not as the disbelievers described them, that they are daughters of Allah.

﴿And indeed they were saying﴾ This is a return to reporting about the polytheists, that is: before the Muhammadan mission, whenever they were overcome by ignorance they would say: ﴿If we had with us a reminder from the earlier ones,﴾ that is: a book from the books of the earlier peoples, such as the Torah and the Gospel, ﴿we would surely have been sincere servants of Allah.﴾ That is: we would have devoted worship to Him and would not have disbelieved in Him.

In His saying "and indeed they were saying," the "in" is the light (mukhaffafah) form of the heavy (thaqilah), in which there is a deleted pronoun of the matter, and the lam is the one that distinguishes it from the negating "in"; that is: indeed the matter was that the disbelievers of the Arabs would say, etc.

The fa' in His saying: ﴿But they disbelieved in it﴾ is the fa' of result (fasihah), indicating a deleted element implied in the speech.

al-Farra' said: its implied meaning is: "then Muhammad came to them with the Reminder, but they disbelieved in it," and this is in the manner of wonder at them.

﴿So they will come to know﴾ That is: the outcome of their disbelief and its end. In this is a severe threat to them.

The clause ﴿And indeed Our word had already preceded for Our servants, the messengers﴾ is a resumed sentence confirming the threat. The "word" means what Allah promised them of victory and triumph over the disbelievers.

Muqatil said: by "the word" He meant His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "Surely I shall prevail, I and My messengers."﴾ [Al-Mujadilah: 21]. al-Farra' said: "Our word preceded with happiness for them." The more preferable view is to interpret this word by what is mentioned here, for He said: ﴿Indeed they are the ones who will be helped, and indeed Our host, they are the ones who will be victorious.﴾ So this word mentioned earlier and this is its explanation. By "the host of Allah" is meant His party, namely the messengers and their followers.

al-Shaybani said: it came here in the plural form: that is, His saying ﴿they are the ones who will be victorious﴾ is because it is the end of a verse. This promise to them of victory and triumph is not contradicted by their defeat in some battles or by the triumph of the disbelievers over them, for the prevailing outcome in every encounter is their victory over the enemies and their triumph over them. So the speech came in the manner of what is usual, and the praiseworthy end is theirs in every condition and in every encounter, as He—glorified is He—said: ﴿And the good end is for the God-fearing.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 128].

Then Allah—glorified is He—commanded His Messenger to turn away from them and to overlook what proceeds from them of ignorance and misguidance, saying: ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ That is: turn away from them for a period known to Allah—glorified is He—which is the period of refraining from fighting. al-Suddi and Mujahid said: until We command you to fight. Qatadah said: until death. It was also said: until the day of Badr; it was also said: until the day of the conquest of Makkah; it was also said: this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿And see them, for they will [soon] see.﴾ That is: and watch them when punishment descends upon them through killing and capture, for they will [soon] see when seeing will not benefit them. He expressed the nearness of the matter by "seeing," that is: they will see in the near future.

It was also said: the meaning is: they will see the punishment on the Day of Resurrection.
